strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: existing text-rich image benchmarks (DocVQA, ChartQA, OCRBench) mostly test extraction/perception rather than multi-step reasoning; the paper convincingly motivates this with Fig. 1 showing only 2.3% of answers are directly retrievable via OCR, versus 78-99% for prior benchmarks.

Novel dual annotation of both final answers and step-by-step reasoning trajectories, enabling process-level (not just outcome-level) evaluation via LLM-as-judge, which is uncommon in prior text-rich benchmarks.

Reasonably fine-grained taxonomy (6 core abilities, 18 practical tasks) with illustrative examples spanning diverse real-world scenarios (financial reports, receipts, schedules, handwritten STEM problems).

Broad and informative experimental evaluation covering OCR+LLM baselines, closed-source MLLMs, open-source MLLMs, and several RL-tuned multimodal reasoning models, yielding several useful empirical observations (importance of visual input over OCR text, inconsistent effect of CoT prompting, weak performance of RL-tuned models, persistent gap between open- and closed-source models on reasoning despite parity on perception benchmarks).

Useful qualitative failure analysis (Figs. 5-6) illustrating concrete error modes (misreading problem context, OCR error propagation, item-name misinterpretation) that add interpretive value beyond aggregate numbers.
weaknesses: Dataset is quite small (1,069 examples over 1,022 images) and unevenly distributed across the six categories (Numerical Analysis 37% vs. Spatial 10%), which limits the statistical reliability of per-category comparisons across ~20 evaluated models.

No inter-annotator agreement or quality-control statistics are reported despite multiple annotation/curation stages (question selection, reasoning-path scoring, category voting), making it hard to assess annotation reliability and benchmark label quality.

The reasoning-process evaluation relies entirely on an LLM-as-judge (unspecified base model), with no validation against human ratings or discussion of judge bias/consistency, despite the paper's own admission in the limitations that such biases are a known issue.

Part of the reasoning-path annotation is generated by Gemini-2.0-Flash and then merely 'scored' against a human-written path, which could bias the benchmark's reference solutions toward the style/errors of a specific proprietary model rather than being purely human-authored ground truth.

About 29% of images are reused from existing benchmarks (InfoVQA, DocVQA, ChartQA, CharXiv, WildReceipt, MME-Finance); no analysis of potential data leakage/contamination with respect to models that may have been pretrained or fine-tuned on these source datasets.

No human performance baseline is reported, which would substantially strengthen the central claim that the benchmark is 'genuinely hard' rather than simply exploiting model weaknesses (e.g., ambiguous question phrasing, format-matching brittleness).

The paper is purely a benchmark/evaluation contribution with no new method or mitigation proposed; overlap with other recent 'reasoning benchmark' papers (e.g., ContextuaL, SEED-Bench-2-Plus, VisuLogic) is acknowledged only narratively, without a systematic comparison table clarifying unique task coverage.

Some categories appear conceptually overlapping (e.g., Mathematical Reasoning vs. Multidisciplinary Knowledge Reasoning both include function/geometry-adjacent STEM problems), raising questions about the taxonomy's discriminative validity beyond what majority-vote annotation captures.

Minor reporting inconsistencies (e.g., Table 3 text states GPT-4o CoT improvement of '9.2%... and 1.0% on GPT-4o' appears to be a typo/duplicate reference) suggest limited proofreading rigor in the results discussion.
